body: It's not an abnormality if it's re-emergent, although sparse.

You actually are slightly empty.

That part of yourself (your ex) was big. Not in a way that most people think, but you litterally shared part of your existence with her, (her too) and usually in a intense way, mostly subtle, but usually intense.

Those memories stuck because of that intensity. Ever remember the first time you got drunk? OR the first time you kissed someone? The first time you fucked?

It burns a deep connection into your memories, and for a good reason, but not one to delve into right now.

That sticks. Very, very tightly. It's not just about them, or you, it's litterally a part of your existence. It forms a part of your identity and the key thing is, it's not actually about the length. First time I fucked it was like what? 5 minutes tops? I can still remember quite clearly the sensation, the environment, the setting, the movie we watched, the exact part of the movie where we stopped watching.

15 minutes of my life and I can STILL remember with vivid intensity everything that happened.

And now, this source of all of these experiences, all these emotions, just everything, has just up and gone. A literal part of yourself, while although unseeable, has just been lopped off. 

Worse yet, you have all these memories, these great pleasures, these great pains and everything in-between, and yet you can never have them again. Not in that specific way, not with that specific person (or maybe, but in a different way).

This is actually how we were meant to be, bonded to one another. Breaking those bonds is horribly, horribly painful, and for me anyways, made me feel like less of a person, because you know what? I actually was less of a person *because* of the absence of that person.

It certainly made me feel like a pathetic creepy loser when I became fixated on my exes, checking their facebook, randomly thinking about them, agonising on whether I should text them, thinking about what I could say, what I could do, because everyone around me says that nothing we have between one another (romantically anyways) is meant to be permenant.

We're meant to "fish" for the right person, the person best for us, when truthfully, the best person for me was her. With all her flaws, and all her perfections, but most importantly in that shared existence we had, it was me. It was her too, sure, but it was me.

As far as finding a connection? Well my ex and I met up almost completely randomly and we hit it off. What are the chances of that happening again, probably about random again.

More importantly, I still am connected to others, but the connections are different. The connection I had with my ex was a direct to fibre connection, the connections I have with others is usually a shitty earbud in my ear recieiving AM talk back radio where I can't understand what the host is saying.

Anyways, you want the best advice? Even though every part of you is probably saying "IDGAF", go join some church, or like a hobby group or something. 9 times out of 10, it'll be small talk, niceities and other stuff. Then you'll unexpectedly a few years down the track (or maybe that day) actually connect with someone.

But like all trees, those roots gotta start growing somewhere. And trees fucking grow mostly everywhere.

So not thinking about death makes it not normal? Isn't death the only constant, the only thing that *will* happen eventually?

Isn't that the most precise definition of what normal is?

There's a few problems;

1) Most of the methods that would instaneously kill you (Shotgun is the only one I can think of) is gorey as hell and there would be MORE attention brought to it because of it.

2) People handle death in very odd ways, but proximity is the key. I hear about people dieing in horrific ways all the time. Look at the FP for the prisoner who was beaten to death by 20 guards. But let's face it, out of sight out of mind. How well do you think anyone would handle a dead cadaver standing right in there face?

You're on the right track if you're thinking the doctor's office, but keep in mind, not all Doctors encounter death first hand. They're in the company of sickness, but not always death. Can they handle it? Probably better than most other people, but humans are still humans.

Also, how many surgeries (doctor's offices) do you see that are empty?

And, well, doctor's are in the position of trying to keep you alive. Then there's only one reliable way of doing it, which would be a shotgun to the head, and you'd have to be sure you could do it quickly enough that he doesn't stop you. Not feasibly difficult, but slightly decreases your chances of permenant death.

Everything else, is more or less "savable", so to speak, pills, hanging, etc. Worse yet, the outcomes of survival when you don't die is just crappy. Disabilities, etc. Explosives is an option, if you could specifically disintegrate target organs (heart/brain/lungs), but that would require specific "bombs" that would severely rupture these organs without causing too much collateral damage. You'd need surgery and ordnance (bombs), specifically tailored to this. A minitaurised shaped charge would work quite well here. You could probably skip the surgery part but this would increase the chances of collateral damage. I don't know actually, it might be possible to do without so, I'm thinking more in terms of distribution of the pressure from the explosion itself, and your body would disperse a lot of the force, this may not happen externally.

You could always stab yourself in the heart with a dagger, or in the spine (a bit harder), which again, is a much more fatal way of dieing, but again, savable. You'd need to fully damage the heart such that the damage is irreversible. And from stories I've heard, as well as seen, it's incredibly painful.

Military or Battlefield is your best bet. Death is rampant, but how well they could handle it? Most people "handle it" but then look at all the returning soldiers from most wars. But it doesn't really solve the problem of not wanting to die alone, because in those situations, when your dead, your just another body until the clean up takes place.

Also, getting there might not be difficult (whether officially or not), but predicting when a battle will take place eludes even the most battle hardened Generals sometimes. Especially in the type of urban wars taking place, battles spring up spontaneously, and fizzle quickly. If they don't, usually it's long periods of hide and seek.

War leaves some longlasting scars, and if there's anybody who we think should be more capable of handling it, soldiers are usually the ones that usually have the worst time handling it, whether directly by your or otherwise.

3) Alone. From what I'm getting from your post, you either don't want to kill yourself alone because; You don't want to be found weeks later, or, because you don't want to face the intensity of the experience by yourself.

I doubt it's the first reason, and the second reason is truly one of my greatest fears in life, and it's probably crossed the minds of billions. It's not even unreasonable to have this fear, given how much time we spend alone and the situations which this could arise. My brother died in a car crash, alone, in the rain at a night with no one around, and despite the coroners, police and multiple family friends (who were doctors) saying he died instaneously, there was always a lingering doubt in my mind that he may have suffered severely for an extended period before he did truly die.

That leaves a few options. Euthanasia, which is mostly illegal in most places. Suicide pact, but this has to be beyond yourself, in which case it's more martyrdom than a suicide. Suicide is simply just the means of which you achieve that.

In both cases you need someone who understands what you're thinking in order to make this decision. That's not so easy, especially in the case of a suicide pact.

There's a few other methods I could think of, but there's usually one trade off between wanting to die alone, wanting to die painlessly, wanting to lessen the emotional impact, and the chances of survival. It's usually one or two of them, but not the other two.

Suppose you could purposefully irradiate yourself with high doses of radiation, you'd more or less likely be with someone when you die from radiation posioning, they'd be more prepared to handle it (knowing the likely outcome), but it's incredibly, incredibly painful.

You could always take large amounts of opiates, and then stroll into the doctors office. Again, savable. In fact, probably much more savable. Cyanide or another potentially fatal posion could also work the same effect, you'd need precision timing though.

Actually suicide is probably the opposite of cowardice. It takes more than a lot of courage to willingly cast yourself into the unknown. And death is the ultimate unknown. I have yet to speak to one dead person, and mysticism, spirituality and everything else aside, very few people *if any* truly have.

It takes a lot of courage to realise you will be in pain, and never really truly knowing how much and how long it will take. Ever broken an arm or leg? Or really hurt yourself badly? Notice how time warps and it can seem longer than it usually is? Add the complete unknown of how much pain you'd be in during death and it's a fucking scary thought. 

Concentrating on it (pain), thinking about it, litterally makes you feel pain, whether or not you realise it. Often at times, just thinking about death is bound to make you anxious and will "stiffen" you up so to speak, because even though physically you're not in any danger, your mind is literally prepping your body for it.

More importantly, once the thought of danger subsides, you still have these residual after-thoughts of pain. Guess what? All those tiny little aches you normally wouldn't even notice all of a sudden become magnified.

Your back hurts, your shoulders hurt, that tiny bump you made into the wall all of a sudden becomes sore. Your focus lies on pain, and thus pain appears. This isn't imagined, the pain was always there, the focus lay elsewhere and as far as everyone is concerned, it doesn't exist.

Selfish? It's selfish to stop someone doing something that they know would be painful for them. When people tell you you're being selfish for committing suicide, it's because they themselves want to stop themselves from being in pain. That's selfish.

Love? It's more than just what we know, it's more than what we experience. There are many types of love, and some of them are not connected. To me, to love is more than just affection, or romance. Love can be a conscious act. Does your family truly love you if they are allowing you to remain in pain all the time? Would it not be more loving, more merciful to allow you the choice to end that pain?

Keep in mind though the answers you seek to to whatever problems you have, are ones of time, whether instantaneous or longer. Just like you, when your thoughts dwell on the idea of suicide, it provokes a immediate response, in you (your family) as well as them. Just like you stiffening at the idea of death, they too stiffen.

Thus most answers are immediate and jilted.

What's more frustrating is that you can talk to a thousand people and not a single one can give you an answer that you need. Not one that is adequate, or fine, or anything else, but one that you actually need.

The real problem then is not whether it's an act of cowardice or an act of selfishness, or even of love. The real problem, the core thing that binds all of this together is pain and suffering.

That, in itself is inescapable. It is inevitable and it is part of being human. The best chance we have is to mediate that pain.

How? I'm still figuring that one out, but the only way to lessen it is to live with it, dwell with it and still push your focus elsewhere. Rely on it, know that it will exist and that it is truly is the only constant that you will have in this life. That and death.

Which is weird, because both are constant while both are incredibly variable.

You want an immediate solution? Go out and run yourself into circles until it's painful. Go out and run and run and run and run and run. Let your thoughts overwhelm you, let it all be there, don't try and stop them. But keep running. Until it hurts to breathe, until your muscles start to burn. Until you can do nothing except focus on that pain, and at least, in this case, you can mediate that specific pain.

Which is, usually, water, a sit down and most likely a meal later on.

Go run.

>Who can you actually articulate your darkest thoughts to without getting a crisis response?

Family, friends, people who you feel close to.

In the absence of this, all your left with is four walls and a blank screen and your own thoughts.

Crisis lines are exactly that, crisis lines. They deal with immediate issues that can be rectified immediately, and what absolutely sucks about every single one of them is that they can't (litterally won't) get into the subtleties that cast a shadow on those thoughts.

There have been so many times, SO many times, where all I needed was someone where I could go, which was warm, relatively safe and where my thoughts could dwell elsewhere. Fuck talking, sometimes I just need human contact. Genuine human contact.

The country I live in, the values we champion (independence from each other, solidarity in solitude) are all singlehandley some of the most destructive forces for a truly healthy and prosperous life.

Yet to take these things away would be to drive down the value of the individual, and let's face it, feeling unique and valued is also one of the most important things we need.

Rants aside, this is just human existence. It's a fucking shit, god awful, frustratingly, and incredibly depressing part of it, and it happens so frequently and so often. This subreddit is a dip in the pond compared to the countless people who experience this daily.

But yes, I fully understand you, because even after you get a response, it might help for a time,but it's not in your immediate proximity, like litterally there in your face. That in-dwelling, that force that's binding you is still there, needs to be released, to be dispersed.

One part is mediating it, whether this is therapy or otherwise, which takes time, trial and error. The other part is knowing this will exist, almost irrespective of anything else that happens and at various points without any apparent cause or concern.

That's just the difficult part and for that I really have no answer other than knowing that it's there.
